name: Role + Goal + Format
summary: Open with who Claude is, what it's trying to achieve, and how the output should be structured.
when: Always apply on build-from-scratch. On refine, apply when the prompt lacks any of the three components (role, goal, format).
weak_example: Help me write a marketing email.
strong_example: You are a direct-response copywriter. Your goal is to write a cold email that gets a reply within 48 hours. Format: subject line, 3 short paragraphs, one CTA.
why: Giving Claude a clear identity, objective, and output shape eliminates ambiguity and produces dramatically more focused output.

name: Targeted Negative Constraints
summary: Add explicit exclusions for known failure modes — unwanted patterns the user has already seen or can predict. Pair them with positive instructions, don't replace them.
when: Apply when the user has experienced (or can reliably predict) a specific unwanted pattern in outputs: hedging, bullet-point overuse, generic summaries. Pair each exclusion with the positive alternative where possible ('no bullet points — write in flowing prose'). Avoid blanket negative fencing: positive specificity is the primary lever, and recent Claude models follow instructions literally, so broad 'do not' lists can cause overcorrection.
strong_example: Don't hedge with phrases like 'it depends' — commit to one recommendation. No bullet points; write in flowing prose. Skip the survey of options and go straight to your pick and why.
why: Targeted exclusions are high-leverage when they name a failure mode the model would otherwise drift into. They work best paired with the positive behavior you want — narrowing the output space without inviting overcorrection.

name: Thinking Out Loud Prefix
summary: Add a line before complex tasks that forces Claude to reason before answering.
when: Apply when the task involves judgment, analysis, recommendations, or any situation where a confident wrong answer is worse than a slower right one. Less impactful when the target model has extended thinking enabled — it already reasons before answering. Highest value for API calls without thinking, or non-thinking models.
weak_example: What framework should I use for this project?
strong_example: Before you answer, think through the key variables, competing considerations, and what information would change your recommendation. Then give me your recommendation.
why: This single line reduces confident wrong answers significantly by forcing reasoning before output. It activates deeper analysis rather than pattern-matched responses.

name: Staged Prompting
summary: Break complex tasks into sequential stages (Analyze → Draft → Critique → Refine) rather than asking for everything in one shot.
when: Apply when the task is multi-faceted — writing with research, analysis with recommendations, any output that benefits from self-review. Skip for simple, single-focus tasks.
weak_example: Write me a business plan for a coffee shop.
strong_example: Stage 1: Analyze the competitive landscape for specialty coffee in downtown Austin. Stage 2: Draft the executive summary and financial projections. Stage 3: Critique your own draft — identify the weakest assumptions. Stage 4: Revise based on your critique.
why: Each stage builds on the last. The final output from staged prompting is not comparable to a single-shot attempt because self-critique catches errors and weak reasoning.

name: Specify the Reader
summary: Define who will read the output — not just the topic, but the person, their background, and their context.
when: Apply whenever the output will be read by someone specific (or a specific type of person). Especially high-impact for explanations, persuasive writing, and recommendations.
strong_example: Explain machine learning to a VP of Sales who has zero technical background but needs to make a $200K software decision next week.
why: Claude writes for whoever is reading. A real person with real stakes produces a completely different tone, depth, and framing than a generic topic request.

name: Steel Man the Counter
summary: After getting a recommendation, ask Claude for the strongest possible argument against it.
when: Apply when the user is making a decision, evaluating options, or needs to stress-test a position. Also useful when the user explicitly wants balanced analysis. In the Build path, embed it as a closing instruction inside the prompt itself; as a standalone follow-up message, it works when refining a live conversation.
strong_example: After you give your recommendation, present the strongest possible argument against it. What would a smart skeptic say?
why: You get both sides stress-tested in one conversation. This prevents confirmation bias and surfaces risks the initial recommendation may have glossed over.

name: XML Structure for Complex Inputs
summary: Wrap multi-part inputs in XML tags (<context>, <task>, <constraints>) to sharpen Claude's attention.
when: Apply when the prompt involves long documents, multiple data sources, or multi-part instructions that could blur together without structure.
weak_example: Here's some background info and also here's what I want you to do and by the way keep it under 500 words.
strong_example:
<context>Q3 sales data showing 12% decline in enterprise segment</context>
<task>Write an internal memo explaining the decline and proposing 3 corrective actions</task>
<constraints>Keep under 500 words. No jargon. Audience is the board.</constraints>
why: Claude's attention sharpens when inputs are structurally separated. XML tags prevent context from bleeding into task instructions and vice versa.

name: Surgical Revision
summary: Instead of 'make it better,' target the single weakest element and ask for a specific rewrite with reasoning.
when: Apply during refinement passes. Especially useful when the user says 'improve this' or 'make it better' without specifics.
strong_example: Identify the single weakest sentence in this piece and rewrite only that sentence. Then tell me why it was the weakest.
why: Specific revision targets produce specific improvements. 'Make it better' produces generic polishing. Surgical prompts produce surgical results.

name: Show, Don't Tell
summary: Include 1-3 concrete examples of the desired output directly in the prompt, wrapped in <example> tags.
when: Apply when output quality depends on format, tone, style, or structure that's hard to describe in words. Among the highest-leverage techniques in Anthropic's own guidance. Recent Claude models closely replicate the conventions in provided examples — formatting, naming, punctuation — so make every detail of the example match what you want.
weak_example: Write product descriptions in our brand voice.
strong_example: Write product descriptions in our brand voice. Here's one that nails it: <example>Meet the Birch Side Table. Solid wood, no veneer, no fuss. Assembles in four minutes — we timed it.</example> Match this length, rhythm, and directness.
why: Examples show rather than tell. They communicate subtle requirements that paragraphs of description can't, and they enforce consistent structure and style across outputs.
